https://www.dw.com/en/new-crew-makes-the.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Nc4C SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Cape Canaveral, Florida Image: Philip Scott Andrews/REUTERS Advertisement Four astronauts docked at the International Space Station (ISS) port on Thursday after completing the fastest flight by a US spacecraft to the outpost, NASA officials said. The SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, with the Crew-13 aboard, lifted off at 11:10 a.m. local time (1510 GMT) from Cape Canaveral, Florida, and within 7 hours and 55 minutes, its capsule, SpaceX Dragon "Grace," docked at the ISS — setting a record for a US trip to the ISS. The flight by the spacecraft was the quickest so far, not only for Elon Musk's company, but for any American entity, including NASA. The time taken for a trip to the ISS mainly depends on the distance between the ISS and the spacecraft at the time of launch. The space station's convenient location allowed the spacecraft to reach it faster. A Russian Soyuz spacecraft set the overall record for a flight to the ISS in October 2020, reaching the station in just over three hours. What do we know about the crew? The new ISS crew was set to arrive in mid-September, however, its flight was delayed due to a leak aboard the Dragon. It includes Americans Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Joshua Kutryk, and Russian Sergey Teteryatnikov Watkins, the Crew-13's commander, became the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. The crew is slated to stay at the ISS for six months and will be replacing Crew-12, which is set to return to Earth on Monday. Despite many international cooperation agreements collapsing after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the United States and other ISS partners still work with Russia on the space station. The ISS has been continuously in use for the last 25 years. NASA has committed to operating it through 2030. Don't let the algorithm hide the news. (Alik Keplicz/AP) By JOHN VANDIVER STARS AND STRIPES Published September 24, 2026 · A Russian military helicopter briefly crossed into Poland on Wednesday, prompting fighter jets to scramble in response to the latest in a series of aerial intrusions along NATO’s eastern flank. The Mi-8 helicopter flying from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad penetrated about 350 yards into Polish territory and remained inside the country for 42 seconds, Poland’s operational command said in a statement. “Fighter aircraft were scrambled, and ground-based forces and assets remained on standby,” the command said, adding that the incident was meant to test NATO’s air defense preparedness. The incursion comes amid a flurry of encounters between NATO and Russian aircraft and drones around Poland and elsewhere along the alliance’s eastern edge . A day before the helicopter incident, Polish fighters intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft flying about 30 miles off the Polish coast over the Baltic Sea. “These are not isolated incidents, but an element of constant pressure,” Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said in a statement Tuesday. Early Thursday morning, Romania scrambled two F-16 fighter jets after an unidentified aerial target crossed into the country from Ukraine, the Romanian defense ministry said . Hours earlier, two Spanish F-18s assigned to NATO’s air policing mission in Romania scrambled after radar detected a group of aerial targets over Ukraine near the Romanian border, the statement added. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk last week sounded the alarm over such incidents, saying there are intelligence indications that Russia could use drones or missiles against a NATO country and characterize it as accidental. Such a move would be an attempt to test allies and cause divisions over how to respond, he said. In recent weeks, other European officials have voiced similar concerns about what they say is a wider Russian campaign involving airspace violations, sabotage and cyberattacks. However, some regional officials warned against unnecessary panic. Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna, whose country borders Russia, said Wednesday that there are no indications of a looming Russian attack on NATO. “It’s empty on the other side of Estonia’s border because Russia’s troops are in Ukraine,” Tsahkna said. “Therefore, all the talk about Russia potentially attacking NATO soon is simply not supported by what we see on the ground.” NATO Europe John Vandiver covers U.S. military activities across Europe and Africa.
